title: Acute ischaemic stroke: thrombolysis and thrombectomy
subject: neurology
setting: Prehospital, emergency department, stroke unit, ICU
summary: Time-critical reperfusion: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) within 4.5 hours for disabling deficits with BP below 185/110 mmHg, thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients, then aspirin and stroke unit care.

sections.title: Recognise and triage
items: Sudden focal deficit (face, arm or leg weakness, speech, vision, balance): use BE-FAST or FAST, pre-alert the stroke team and record the exact time last known well (for wake-up stroke, the time last seen normal).
Check capillary glucose immediately: hypoglycaemia below 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) mimics stroke and must be corrected before any thrombolysis decision.
Score NIHSS. Suspect large vessel occlusion (LVO) with gaze deviation, aphasia or neglect, dense hemiparesis or NIHSS 6 or more.

Mimics: post-ictal paresis, migraine aura, hypoglycaemia, functional deficit, sepsis unmasking an old deficit. A seizure at onset does not exclude thrombolysis if the deficit is judged to be from stroke.

sections.title: First 60 minutes (door to needle)
items: Non-contrast CT (or MRI) immediately on arrival, target within 20 to 25 minutes. Do CT angiography from arch to vertex in the same sitting if thrombectomy is possible; do not wait for creatinine.
Add CT perfusion or MRI (DWI-FLAIR, perfusion) for patients beyond 4.5 hours, wake-up stroke or presentation at 6 to 24 hours.

Only blood glucose is required before thrombolysis. Do not wait for platelets or INR unless anticoagulant use, thrombocytopenia or a bleeding disorder is suspected; ECG and troponin must not delay IVT or EVT.
Targets: door to needle under 60 minutes, door to groin puncture under 90 minutes for thrombectomy candidates.
Oxygen only to keep SpO2 above 94%. Isotonic saline; avoid hypotonic or glucose-containing fluids. Nil by mouth until a swallow screen is passed.

sections.title: IV thrombolysis
items: Disabling deficit within 4.5 hours of onset or last known well, CT without haemorrhage or extensive hypodensity: give tenecteplase or alteplase (equally endorsed by AHA/ASA 2026; tenecteplase is a single bolus).

Extended window 4.5 to 9 hours from last known well, or wake-up stroke within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep: thrombolysis is reasonable if perfusion imaging or DWI-FLAIR mismatch shows salvageable tissue.
LVO with salvageable tissue at 4.5 to 24 hours when thrombectomy is not available: tenecteplase may be considered (weak recommendation, AHA/ASA 2026).
Mild non-disabling deficits (for example isolated sensory loss, NIHSS 0 to 5 non-disabling): do not thrombolyse; give dual antiplatelet therapy instead.

Exclusions: any intracranial haemorrhage; previous ICH; ischaemic stroke, severe head injury or intracranial or spinal surgery within 3 months; GI bleed or GI malignancy within 21 days; intra-axial brain tumour; infective endocarditis; aortic arch dissection; symptoms suggesting SAH.
Coagulation exclusions: platelets below 100,000/mm3, INR above 1.7, aPTT above 40 s, PT above 15 s, treatment-dose LMWH within 24 hours, DOAC within 48 hours unless drug-specific tests are normal.
BP must be below 185/110 mmHg before the bolus and kept below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after. If it cannot be brought below 185/110 mmHg, do not thrombolyse.

sections.title: Mechanical thrombectomy
items: ICA or M1 occlusion within 6 hours with NIHSS 6 or more, pre-stroke mRS 0 to 1 and ASPECTS 3 to 10: thrombectomy recommended. Also reasonable with ASPECTS 0 to 2 (age below 80, no significant mass effect) or pre-stroke mRS 2 with ASPECTS 6 or more.

ICA or M1 occlusion at 6 to 24 hours: thrombectomy when imaging shows salvageable tissue by DAWN (clinical-core mismatch, up to 24 hours) or DEFUSE 3 (perfusion mismatch, up to 16 hours) criteria, and for large core ASPECTS 3 to 5 if age below 80, NIHSS 6 or more, mRS 0 to 1 and no significant mass effect.
Basilar artery occlusion within 24 hours: thrombectomy recommended if pre-stroke mRS 0 to 1, NIHSS 10 or more and PC-ASPECTS 6 or more; benefit uncertain at NIHSS 6 to 9.

Medium or distal vessel occlusion: routine thrombectomy is not recommended; the 2025 trials ESCAPE-MeVO and DISTAL showed no benefit. Newer data suggest possible benefit with more severe deficits, so decide case by case with the neurointerventionist.
Give IV thrombolysis first if eligible, without delaying transfer or groin puncture to watch for a response. Transfer directly to a thrombectomy-capable centre.
After thrombectomy keep BP at or below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; do not target systolic BP below 140 mmHg after successful reperfusion (harmful).

sections.title: Antithrombotics and supportive care
items: Aspirin 300 mg orally (rectally or by nasogastric tube if dysphagic) within 24 to 48 hours in patients not thrombolysed. After thrombolysis, give no antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 24 hours; start once the 24-hour scan excludes haemorrhage.

Minor non-cardioembolic stroke not thrombolysed (NIHSS 3 or less, or up to 5 with large artery atherosclerosis): aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, ideally started within 24 hours (up to 72 hours), then a single antiplatelet.
No reperfusion therapy: treat BP only if 220/120 mmHg or higher, lowering by about 15% over the first 24 hours; otherwise allow permissive hypertension.
Keep glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10 mmol/L); treat values below 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L). Tight control to 80 to 130 mg/dL is not recommended.
Treat fever above 38°C and look for infection; formal swallow screen before oral intake; intermittent pneumatic compression for immobile patients; care in a stroke unit.
Atrial fibrillation: early DOAC start after haemorrhage is excluded is reasonable in selected patients (AHA/ASA 2026); agree the timing with the stroke team according to infarct size.

sections.title: After thrombolysis
items: Neurological checks and BP every 15 minutes for 2 hours, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly to 24 hours. Repeat CT or MRI at 24 hours before antithrombotics.
New headache, vomiting, worsening deficit or acute hypertension: stop the infusion, urgent CT, send CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and crossmatch.

Symptomatic ICH after thrombolysis: cryoprecipitate 10 units IV (repeat if fibrinogen below 150 mg/dL) or tranexamic acid 10 to 15 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes; urgent neurosurgical and haematology input.

Orolingual angioedema (higher risk with ACE inhibitors): stop the infusion, hold ACE inhibitor, give IV methylprednisolone 125 mg and an antihistamine; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg if progressing; secure the airway early.
Avoid nasogastric tubes, urinary catheters and arterial punctures at non-compressible sites in the first 24 hours where safely possible.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Children 28 days to 18 years (AHA/ASA 2026): alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours may be considered for disabling deficits; thrombectomy may be considered for LVO in children aged 6 years and older. Involve paediatric stroke specialists.

India: tenecteplase is widely available. Check the vial strength and draw up the stroke dose (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg), never the cardiac dose. Where thrombectomy is not available locally, thrombolyse and transfer.

Large MCA infarction with swelling: refer early for decompressive hemicraniectomy (within 48 hours; strongest benefit at age 60 or below). Cerebellar infarction with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus: urgent neurosurgery.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving the cardiac tenecteplase dose (up to 50 mg by weight band) for stroke.
Delaying thrombolysis for routine bloods, ECG, troponin or chest X-ray.
Over-lowering BP: below 220/120 mmHg in untreated patients, or systolic below 140 mmHg after reperfusion.
Missing hypoglycaemia or aortic dissection (chest or back pain, pulse or BP differential) before thrombolysis.

drugs.name: Tenecteplase
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV single bolus over 5 to 10 seconds (max 25 mg)
drugs.notes: Within 4.5 hours, or extended window with imaging selection. Stroke dose only: never use the STEMI weight-band dose (30 to 50 mg).

drugs.name: Alteplase
drugs.dose: 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg): 10% as bolus over 1 minute, remaining 90% infused over 60 minutes
drugs.notes: Children 28 days to 18 years: 0.9 mg/kg may be considered (AHA/ASA 2026).

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes, may repeat once; or 10 mg IV then infusion 2 to 8 mg/min
drugs.notes: To bring BP below 185/110 mmHg before, and below 180/105 mmHg after, reperfusion. Avoid in asthma, heart block, bradycardia.

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.dose: 5 mg/h IV infusion, increase by 2.5 mg/h every 5 to 15 minutes, max 15 mg/h
drugs.notes: Alternative to labetalol; availability varies in India.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.dose: 300 mg orally, rectally or by NG tube within 24 to 48 hours, then 75 to 150 mg daily
drugs.notes: After thrombolysis start after the 24-hour scan. NICE continues 300 mg daily for 2 weeks.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel (with aspirin)
drugs.dose: 300 to 600 mg orally loading, then 75 mg daily for 21 days
drugs.notes: Minor non-cardioembolic stroke not thrombolysed; then single antiplatelet.

drugs.name: Cryoprecipitate
drugs.dose: 10 units IV; repeat if fibrinogen below 150 mg/dL

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.notes: Alternative or adjunct for thrombolysis-related ICH.
